newsitem.title: GERMANY: German deficit overshoot won't delay EMU - analysts.
newsitem.headline: German deficit overshoot won't delay EMU - analysts.

text.p: The German government still has time to take the knife to next year's budget and cut the state deficit enough to enable European monetary union to go ahead as planned in 1999, economists said on Tuesday.

Germany's six top economic institutes said in their autumn forecast that the 1997 deficit would be 3.5 percent of gross domestic product, above the the Maastricht Treaty's three-percent goal for joining monetary union in 1999.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, an advocate of a strict reading of the treaty, said "the conditions will be created" in final budget talks to bring the deficit below three percent.
Parliament's budget committee will review a final draft on November 14 to submit to parliament.
Waigel has been under fire for weeks after the Social Democrat (SPD) opposition wrecked his 1997 tax bill and junior coalition partners the Free Democrats (FDP) blocked tax hikes.
Waigel now has little time to find three billion marks ($2 billion) he says needs to be saved.
But analysts said Waigel, facing a budget hole running into billions of marks, would probably not hit the target.
"We are going to stay over," Gerhard Grebe, chief economist at Bank Julius Baer in Frankfurt, told Reuters.
"I expect Waigel will consolidate more, but he will have difficulty in fulfilling the Maastricht criteria," he said.

But with Maastricht offering the possibility of a looser reading, requiring only that deficits are going in the right direction, Germany is sure to be in the first wave of countries to launch the euro currency, the analysts said.

"Discussions over a strict interpretation of the Maastricht criteria (will become) more sensitive. Monetary union certainly can't start without Germany," said Karen Kricks-Brunnlieb, head of bond analysis at Trinkaus & Burkhardt.
Ruetger Teuscher, economist at Deutsche Bank Research, said that although German state finances were in a critical state, there was no question of monetary union being delayed.
"I wouldn't add my voice to those talking of a failure of the whole convergence process," Teuscher said.
Analysts also said that despite bitter coalition squabbling and opposition attacks, there is a political consensus in Germany that European monetary union is a worthwhile project.
That should enable a compromise on spending cuts, however hard-fought, to be struck.
"All political parties support monetary union in 1999 and want the Maastricht criteria to be fulfilled," said Pieter Pietsch, economist at Commerzbank.
Grebe said that, with inflation at its lowest levels in Germany since the mid-1980s and falling throughout Europe, the deficits were being overplayed as a factor.
More importantly now was ensuring that a stability pact proposed by Waigel to enforce EMU discipline is agreed with real sanctions against countres which let state finances slip.
"Look, we are overshooting on the deficit, but we will have a stability pact with teeth to discipline peripheral currencies and guarantee stability," Grebe said.
Other key elements of the forecast by the six institutes were well within economists' expectations.
The institutes said GDP would grow by 1.5 percent this year, accelerating to 2.5 percent next year.

Inflation is expected to stay subdued at 1.5 percent, but recovery will have little impact on unemployment next year, which will average four million, or 10.4 percent of the workforce. ($1=1.5130 Mark)
